5	\label{sec:conclusion}

7	We presented a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as model collapse severity monitors.
8	Across three experimental configurations spanning two model scales (0.5B, 1.5B), two fine-tuning methods (QLoRA, full fine-tuning), and six contamination fractions on WikiText-2, we established three findings.
9	
10	First, spectral and output signals reliably track collapse severity across configurations.
11	Spectral entropy achieves the largest and most reproducible effect size ($d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
12	Six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.
13	
14	Second, stable rank provides within-generation early warning, achieving $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled) and 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
15	Train loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), though its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data rather than improved model quality.
16	Held-out evaluation perplexity (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$) and token entropy (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$) fail at within-generation detection---the most commonly relied-upon quality metric is no better than chance at the most actionable task.
17	
18	Third, signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale, motivating a three-tier monitoring strategy: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.
19

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

As LLM-generated text pervades web-scraped training corpora, practitioners increasingly fine-tune models on data shaped by prior model generations.
This recursive dynamic creates self-consuming loops that cause \emph{model collapse}---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
The problem compounds: even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse at sufficient depth~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors accumulating across iterations at accelerating rates~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}.
Yet the metric practitioners most commonly rely on for quality assessment---held-out evaluation perplexity---fails to detect this degradation within a run, achieving pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation collapse detection (indistinguishable from random chance).
Train loss does change under collapse (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), but its decrease is interpretively ambiguous: the model fits lower-entropy synthetic data more easily, which looks like healthy convergence.
A practitioner watching only perplexity or interpreting train loss at face value would have no reliable warning that collapse is underway.

Existing work addresses model collapse from two directions.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Shumailov2024} established the phenomenon, \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved that any nonzero synthetic fraction eventually induces strong collapse, and \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed that collapse alters neural scaling laws.
On the mitigation side, data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, and verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025} each reduce collapse pressure under specific conditions.
Missing from this landscape is a systematic analysis of which \emph{training-time signals} best track collapse severity, when they provide early warning, and where they saturate or actively mislead.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} highlight that even the definition of collapse varies across studies, further motivating signal-level analysis grounded in controlled experiments.
The two closest concurrent works---SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026}, which monitors output embedding spectra, and the topological index of \citet{Kalinowski2026}---each address part of this gap but carry limitations: SIGMA requires a clean reference distribution and operates post-hoc; topological monitoring incurs higher computational cost.
Neither provides a cross-family comparison of signal operating ranges or quantitative within-generation early warning thresholds.

We conduct a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as collapse severity monitors.
We evaluate four signal families---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (train loss, evaluation perplexity, token entropy), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---across three experimental configurations spanning two model scales (0.5B, 1.5B), two fine-tuning methods (QLoRA and full fine-tuning), and six contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$) on WikiText-2.
Our central finding is that different signal families have complementary operating ranges, and the same signal's utility can flip from informative to misleading depending on the training method.

Our contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Signal--severity correlation.}
    Spectral and output signals track collapse across contamination levels.
    Spectral entropy achieves the largest effect size (Cohen's $d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
    Validated across QLoRA and full fine-tuning, six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.
    The exception---gradient norm, which is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning---demonstrates that method-dependence is a first-order concern for monitoring pipeline design.

    \item \textbf{Within-generation early warning and negative results.}

    Train loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), though its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data rather than improved model quality.
    Held-out evaluation perplexity achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation detection---the most commonly relied-upon quality metric fails at the most actionable task---and token entropy achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$, providing no reliable discrimination despite a large initial deviation.

    \item \textbf{Signal taxonomy with method-dependent operating ranges.}
    Signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale.
    Gradient norm is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning.

    Full fine-tuning produces sharper collapse onset ($15.3\times$ evaluation perplexity ratio at generation~1) than QLoRA ($8.7\times$) but lower terminal severity.
    These findings motivate a three-tier recommendation: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.
\end{enumerate}

Section~\ref{sec:related_work} surveys collapse theory, spectral analysis of neural networks, and concurrent monitoring approaches.
Section~\ref{sec:method} details our iterative contamination protocol, signal definitions, and evaluation framework.
Section~\ref{sec:results} presents signal--severity correlations, within-generation early warning analysis, and the method-dependent signal taxonomy.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses practical monitoring recommendations and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as model collapse severity monitors.
Across three experimental configurations spanning two model scales (0.5B, 1.5B), two fine-tuning methods (QLoRA, full fine-tuning), and six contamination fractions on WikiText-2, we established three findings.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Practical Three-Tier Monitoring Recommendation}
\label{sec:three_tier}

No single signal suffices for collapse monitoring across all operating regimes.
Our results motivate a three-tier strategy that assigns each signal family to the task where it excels:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Within-generation alarm} $\to$ stable rank.
    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled), with $\Delta_\mathrm{SR} = 34.4\%$ at step~50 (3\% of training).
    This structural sensitivity---detecting energy dispersal across representation dimensions before output-level metrics respond---provides the earliest actionable warning.

    \item \textbf{Cross-generation severity tracking} $\to$ evaluation perplexity.
    With a large absolute effect size ($d = 20.82$) and monotonic growth across generations, evaluation perplexity provides an interpretable severity scale that maps directly to language modeling quality on held-out text.

    \item \textbf{Severity discrimination} $\to$ spectral entropy.
    The largest effect size ($d = 33.48$) and lowest coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$) across seeds make spectral entropy the most reproducible discriminator between contamination levels.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent
This assignment reflects a core finding: the signal that best detects collapse onset (stable rank, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$, seed-sensitive) differs from the one that most reproducibly quantifies its severity (spectral entropy).

\subsection{Evaluation Perplexity: Within-Generation Failure Mechanism}
\label{sec:ppl_failure}

Evaluation perplexity achieves only overall $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$---indistinguishable from chance---despite being the primary severity indicator across generations.
As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}, this failure is structural: collapse pressure enters only at the next generation, so evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation through the iterative loop, not within a single run.
Train loss ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$ at completion) is the second-strongest within-generation signal, but its trajectory reveals early-training direction reversal: AUROC starts at $0.24$ at 10\% progress (below chance) because the collapsing model's loss is initially \emph{lower}, recovering only as cumulative degradation raises loss in the second half of training (Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results}).
For practitioners, the implication is that evaluation perplexity is a lagging indicator of collapse, and train loss changes require spectral cross-validation to interpret correctly.

\subsection{Partial Recovery at Moderate Contamination}
\label{sec:recovery}

The partial recovery at moderate contamination documented in Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy} is consistent with data accumulation effects~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}: the retained real data fraction attenuates collapse pressure.
The practical consequence is that monitoring thresholds should be calibrated to the expected contamination level rather than set as binary decisions.

\subsection{Comparison with Concurrent Monitoring Approaches}
\label{sec:sigma_comparison}

The signals evaluated here incur near-zero marginal cost: they are computed from quantities already available during standard training and require no clean reference distribution.
SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026} operates post-hoc on the output embedding Gram matrix and requires a clean reference distribution for comparison.
\citet{Kalinowski2026} uses persistent homology, incurring higher computational cost from a different signal family entirely.
Neither provides the systematic comparison of signal families, operating range characterization across contamination fractions, or within-generation early warning documented here.
These approaches are complementary: SIGMA and topological methods may capture aspects of collapse that spectral covariance signals miss, while our signals offer the advantage of online, reference-free monitoring integrated into the training loop.

\subsection{Terminal Spectral Convergence}
\label{sec:terminal_convergence}

Terminal stable rank values at generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$ are strikingly similar across methods: $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full FT) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA), a 1.2\% difference despite divergent output-level severity.
This observation rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence; see Appendix~\ref{app:terminal_convergence} for discussion.
```

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model collapse in iterative training.}
Model collapse---progressive degradation when models train on their own outputs---has been established across generative families~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
Theoretical analyses show that even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors compounding across iterations~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}, altered scaling laws~\citep{Seddik2024}, and entropy-driven memorization transitions~\citep{Shi2025_neurips}.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} catalogued eight distinct collapse definitions, motivating precise operationalization.
Mitigation strategies include data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024,Kazdan2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025,Yi2025}, and correction functions~\citep{Gillman2024,Bakshi2026}.
These works establish \emph{that} collapse occurs and \emph{how} to mitigate it, but rely on post-hoc evaluation; none provides real-time training-time monitoring.

\paragraph{Spectral and training-dynamic diagnostics.}
Spectral properties of weight matrices predict model quality without test data~\citep{Martin2021}, with stable rank linked to generalization~\citep{Sanyal2020} and shown to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}.
Recent work has characterized spectral dynamics across training~\citep{Liu2026_lifecycle,Staats2024,Pennington2017}, used spectral signals for compression and pruning~\citep{Xu2026,AlphaPruning2024,Yunis2024}, and applied gradient-based diagnostics~\citep{Li2025_gradient,Elgaar2026}, diffusion spectral entropy~\citep{Chen2024_dse}, spectral alignment~\citep{Qiu2025}, and loss landscape curvature~\citep{Kalra2026} to training health monitoring.

\paragraph{Closest concurrent work.}
SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026} analyzes the output embedding Gram matrix spectrum to quantify collapse but operates post-hoc, requires a clean reference distribution, and has not been validated in iterative settings.
\citet{Kalinowski2026} proposes an online topological monitor via persistent homology but uses a different signal family and incurs higher computational cost (Table~\ref{tab:competitor_comparison} in Appendix~\ref{app:competitor_comparison}).
Neither provides a cross-family comparison, documents where signals saturate or mislead, or establishes within-generation early warning thresholds.

\paragraph{Data quality and contamination detection.}
Watermarking~\citep{Kirchenbauer2023,Dathathri2024,Sander2024} and statistical detection~\citep{Mitchell2023,Shi2024_mink} identify synthetic data presence, while dataset-level approaches address quality filtering~\citep{Penedo2024,Zhang2026} and diversity quantification~\citep{Gambetta2024,Wang2025_scaling}.
These methods answer whether synthetic data is \emph{present}; our work addresses how severely it has \emph{degraded} the model, operating in real time during training rather than post-hoc.
Across the literature, no prior work simultaneously achieves online monitoring, spectral/entropic training-dynamic signals, and validation in the iterative synthetic data setting.
```

**limitations.tex:**
```latex
Our study has several limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.

\paragraph{Scale.}
All reported results use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models.
Scale validation at 3B and cross-domain validation on PubMed are ongoing but not yet complete.
Whether signal--severity relationships and operating ranges transfer to models at scales of practical deployment ($\geq$7B) remains unvalidated.
Stable rank baselines are known to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}, and threshold calibration may require per-scale adjustment.

\paragraph{Seed count and statistical power.}
Cross-generation effect sizes are computed from $N = 3$ seeds (C2 configuration, interim 3 of 5 planned seeds); within-generation AUROC results use $N = 1$ seed at 0.5B (C1).
The full fine-tuning comparison (C4) uses $N = 1$ seed.
These sample sizes are insufficient for rank-based tests (minimum $p = 0.25$ for Wilcoxon with $N = 3$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals.
Stable rank's coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$) is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's ($0.0015$), and its effect size dropped from $d = 61.7$ to $d = 9.43$ when a third seed was added---underscoring that our ranking of signals by sensitivity may shift with more seeds.

\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
All reported results use WikiText-2; cross-domain validation on PubMed is ongoing.
Whether our signal taxonomy generalizes to biomedical text, code, dialogue, multilingual text, or instruction-following data is unknown.

\paragraph{Collapse source.}
Our iterative retraining protocol simulates a specific collapse mechanism---self-consuming loops with controlled contamination fractions.
Real-world collapse may involve mixed provenance (multiple model generations), distribution shift between generations, or partial synthetic contamination at unknown fractions.
Signal behavior under these conditions may differ from our controlled setting.

\paragraph{Fine-tuning methods.}
We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.

\paragraph{Causal claims.}
We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.
The spectral entropy increase under collapse reflects a change in representation structure, but we do not prove that this change causes (rather than accompanies) output degradation.
```

1	% Method section — collapse_severity_monitor
2	
3	\section{Methodology}
4	\label{sec:method}
5	
6	We design a controlled framework to evaluate how training-time signals track model collapse severity under iterative synthetic data contamination.
7	Our protocol varies contamination level and generational depth while monitoring four families of signals across three primary experimental configurations (with two additional configurations for ongoing cross-domain and scale validation).
8	
9	\subsection{Iterative Training Protocol}
10	\label{sec:protocol}
11	
12	We simulate iterative model collapse through a multi-generation fine-tuning loop.
13	Let $M_0$ denote a pretrained base model and $\mathcal{D}_\text{real}$ a corpus of real text.
14	At each generation $g \in \{0, 1, \ldots, G{-}1\}$ (with $G=5$), we execute three steps:
15	
16	\begin{enumerate}
17	    \item \textbf{Fine-tune.} Initialize from $M_0$ and fine-tune on the current training corpus $\mathcal{D}_g$, yielding model $\tilde{M}_g$. During training, we collect monitoring signals every 50 optimizer steps via a callback on a held-out validation set (Section~\ref{sec:signals}).
18	    \item \textbf{Generate.} Sample synthetic text $\mathcal{S}_g$ from $\tilde{M}_g$ by prompting with the first 32 tokens of randomly subsampled chunks from $\mathcal{D}_\text{real}$ and generating up to 480 new tokens with nucleus sampling ($p=0.95$, temperature $\tau=1.0$). We subsample 1{,}500 chunks for generation.
19	    \item \textbf{Mix.} Construct the next-generation corpus by replacing fraction $\alpha$ of real chunks with synthetic chunks:
20	    \begin{equation}
21	        \mathcal{D}_{g+1} = (1 - \alpha)\,\mathcal{D}_\text{real} \cup \alpha\,\mathcal{S}_g.
22	        \label{eq:mixing}
23	    \end{equation}
24	\end{enumerate}
25	
26	\noindent
27	Each generation initializes from the \emph{same} pretrained weights $M_0$, isolating the effect of data contamination from cumulative weight drift.
28	Collapse pressure enters solely through the training corpus: at generation $g$, the synthetic component was produced by a model trained on data that itself contained synthetic text from generation $g{-}1$.
29	
30	All fine-tuning runs use AdamW with learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$, weight decay $0.01$, linear warmup over $5\%$ of steps, and gradient clipping at $\|\cdot\|_2 \leq 1.0$.
31	We train for 5 epochs with effective batch size 16 (per-device batch 4, gradient accumulation 4) in \texttt{bf16} mixed precision.
32	QLoRA configurations~\citep{dettmers2023qlora} use rank $r=16$ with adapters on all linear projections and 4-bit NF4 quantization (full details in Appendix~\ref{app:hyperparams}).
33	Full fine-tuning (C4; Table~\ref{tab:configs}) uses identical optimizer settings with all parameters trainable.
34	
35	\subsection{Contamination Fractions}

1	% Limitations section — collapse_severity_monitor
2	
3	Our study has several limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.
4	
5	\paragraph{Scale.}
6	All reported results use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models.
7	Scale validation at 3B and cross-domain validation on PubMed are ongoing but not yet complete.
8	Whether signal--severity relationships and operating ranges transfer to models at scales of practical deployment ($\geq$7B) remains unvalidated.
9	Stable rank baselines are known to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}, and threshold calibration may require per-scale adjustment.
10	
11	\paragraph{Seed count and statistical power.}
12	Cross-generation effect sizes are computed from $N = 3$ seeds (C2 configuration, interim 3 of 5 planned seeds); within-generation AUROC results use $N = 1$ seed at 0.5B (C1).
13	The full fine-tuning comparison (C4) uses $N = 1$ seed.
14	These sample sizes are insufficient for rank-based tests (minimum $p = 0.25$ for Wilcoxon with $N = 3$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals.
15	Stable rank's coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$) is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's ($0.0015$), and its effect size dropped from $d = 61.7$ to $d = 9.43$ when a third seed was added---underscoring that our ranking of signals by sensitivity may shift with more seeds.
16	
17	\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
18	All reported results use WikiText-2; cross-domain validation on PubMed is ongoing.
19	Whether our signal taxonomy generalizes to biomedical text, code, dialogue, multilingual text, or instruction-following data is unknown.
20	
21	\paragraph{Collapse source.}
22	Our iterative retraining protocol simulates a specific collapse mechanism---self-consuming loops with controlled contamination fractions.
23	Real-world collapse may involve mixed provenance (multiple model generations), distribution shift between generations, or partial synthetic contamination at unknown fractions.
24	Signal behavior under these conditions may differ from our controlled setting.
25	
26	\paragraph{Fine-tuning methods.}
27	We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
28	Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.
29	
30	\paragraph{Causal claims.}
31	We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.
32	The spectral entropy increase under collapse reflects a change in representation structure, but we do not prove that this change causes (rather than accompanies) output degradation.

All reported results use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models.

\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
All reported results use WikiText-2; cross-domain validation on PubMed is ongoing.

We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.

\paragraph{Causal claims.}
We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.

% Limitations section — collapse_severity_monitor

Our study has several limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.

\paragraph{Scale.}
All reported results use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models.
Scale validation at 3B and cross-domain validation on PubMed are ongoing but not yet complete.
Whether signal--severity relationships and operating ranges transfer to models at scales of practical deployment ($\geq$7B) remains unvalidated.
Stable rank baselines are known to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}, and threshold calibration may require per-scale adjustment.

\paragraph{Seed count and statistical power.}
Cross-generation effect sizes are computed from $N = 3$ seeds (C2 configuration, interim 3 of 5 planned seeds); within-generation AUROC results use $N = 1$ seed at 0.5B (C1).
The full fine-tuning comparison (C4) uses $N = 1$ seed.
These sample sizes are insufficient for rank-based tests (minimum $p = 0.25$ for Wilcoxon with $N = 3$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals.
Stable rank's coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$) is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's ($0.0015$), and its effect size dropped from $d = 61.7$ to $d = 9.43$ when a third seed was added---underscoring that our ranking of signals by sensitivity may shift with more seeds.

\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
All reported results use WikiText-2; cross-domain validation on PubMed is ongoing.
Whether our signal taxonomy generalizes to biomedical text, code, dialogue, multilingual text, or instruction-following data is unknown.

\paragraph{Repetition confound.}
At $\alpha = 1.0$, the 1{,}500 unique synthetic chunks are upsampled to 4{,}916, introducing repetition (${\sim}3.3\times$ per epoch) that may independently contribute to observed training dynamics beyond synthetic data quality alone.
This confound is absent at $\alpha \leq 0.5$, where unique sample counts are higher.

\paragraph{Collapse source.}
Our iterative retraining protocol simulates a specific collapse mechanism---self-consuming loops with controlled contamination fractions.
Real-world collapse may involve mixed provenance (multiple model generations), distribution shift between generations, or partial synthetic contamination at unknown fractions.
Signal behavior under these conditions may differ from our controlled setting.

\paragraph{Fine-tuning methods.}
We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.

\paragraph{Causal claims.}
We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.
The spectral entropy increase under collapse reflects a change in representation structure, but we do not prove that this change causes (rather than accompanies) output degradation.
